notes:
Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest value in a square matrix sorted by rows and columns; duplicates count separately.
Idea: Binary-search the numeric value range between the top-left and bottom-right entries.
Technique and why it applies: check(m) walks each row from the right, moving left past values greater than m; the remaining prefix contributes its count of values at most m. The outer search finds the smallest value whose cumulative count reaches k.
Invariant: beg is a lower bound on the answer and end remains a value at least as large as the kth smallest.
Edge cases: The matrix is assumed nonempty and square, as the code uses matrix[0][0] and one dimension n.
Complexity: Each check is O(n) because its column pointer only moves left across rows; binary search uses O(log V) checks over value range V. Total is O(n log V) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the kth smallest entry from a row-and-column sorted matrix without storing all n² values.
Idea: Merge matrix values in ascending order using a min-heap of frontier cells.
Technique and why it applies: Starting at the top-left, each popped cell exposes its right neighbor; cells in the first column also expose the next row's first cell. This maintains a heap frontier of candidates.
Invariant: Every heap entry is an unprocessed cell that is next in its row or at the start of a row, and each pop advances the sorted sequence.
Edge cases: The helper includes dimension checks for rectangular matrices, though the stated problem is square. k must be valid and the matrix nonempty.
Complexity: At most k values are popped and a constant number of cells are pushed per pop, giving O(k log n) time and O(n) heap space for the frontier.

Task and constraints: Decide whether ransomNote can be assembled from magazine letters, using each magazine occurrence at most once.
Idea: Count the characters in each string and compare required frequencies with available frequencies.
Technique and why it applies: Counter creates occurrence counts. For every required character, the code checks that magazine contains at least that many copies; a missing character or insufficient count returns False.
Invariant: Every required character checked so far has enough available occurrences, or the method has already returned False.
Edge cases: An empty ransom note returns True because its count map is empty. The early False after the inner condition is aligned with the loop body, so insufficient counts are rejected.
Complexity: Counting and comparison take O(m+n) expected time for lengths m and n, with O(u) auxiliary storage for distinct characters in both counters.

Task and constraints: Check whether the letters in ransomNote can be supplied by magazine without reusing any occurrence.
Idea: Subtract the magazine Counter from the ransom-note Counter and test whether the result is empty.
Technique and why it applies: Counter subtraction retains only positive frequency differences, so an empty result means no character is required more often than it is available.
Invariant: The expression represents exactly the character deficits after accounting for magazine frequencies.
Edge cases: Empty ransomNote yields an empty Counter difference and therefore True. Characters absent from magazine remain as positive deficits.
Complexity: Constructing the counters and subtracting them takes O(m+n) expected time and O(u) space for distinct characters. The implementation relies on the usual lowercase-English input alphabet only for the task, not for its counting method.

Task and constraints: Determine whether magazine contains enough occurrences of every lowercase letter needed by ransomNote.
Idea: Track each letter's deficit in a fixed 26-element array and stop once all required letter types are satisfied.
Technique and why it applies: The first pass counts ransomNote letters and tracks how many distinct required letters remain unmet. The magazine pass decrements counts; when a count reaches zero, one required letter type is fully supplied.
Invariant: letters counts required character types whose remaining deficit is positive.
Edge cases: If ransomNote is empty, letters remains zero and the result is True. The code assumes lowercase English letters.
Complexity: Both strings are scanned once, so time is O(m+n), or O(n) if n denotes their combined length. The fixed-size counter gives O(1) auxiliary space, matching the author labels.

Task and constraints: Return integers from 1 through n in lexicographical order; the stated target is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
Idea: Insert each decimal representation into a digit trie, then traverse the trie in digit order.
Technique and why it applies: Prefixes are emitted before their descendants, and iterating child keys in insertion order follows numeric digit insertion order for this loop.
Invariant: The trie represents every string from 1 through n, with each number stored along its digit path.
Edge cases: n=1 yields [1]. The implementation stores a trie node for each digit prefix and recursively traverses it, so it does not meet the O(1) extra-space requirement; traversal order depends on dictionary insertion order.
Complexity: Inserting all numbers costs O(n log n) digit work in the worst case, and trie storage is O(total digits), up to O(n log n), plus the O(n) output. It does not achieve the stated bounds.

Task and constraints: Return the index of the first character that occurs exactly once, or -1 if every character repeats.
Idea: For each position, count that character's occurrences in the whole string and return the first index with count one.
Technique and why it applies: s.count performs a full scan for each tested character; because positions are examined left to right, the first successful index is the required answer.
Invariant: Every earlier position has already been shown to contain a character that repeats.
Edge cases: The code returns -1 when all characters repeat. The unused ls list has no effect.
Complexity: Each s.count costs O(n), and up to n positions may be tested, yielding O(n²) time. Apart from a few variables, auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Find the first non-repeating character's index, or return -1 if no such character exists.
Idea: Count characters while tracking candidate positions for characters seen exactly once so far.
Technique and why it applies: lookup stores the first index plus one for each character. A repeated character removes that stored candidate; the set's minimum remaining position is the earliest unique character.
Invariant: candidtates contains encoded indices of characters encountered exactly once, while lookup identifies first occurrences.
Edge cases: A character appearing three or more times is discarded on its second occurrence and never re-added. If no candidates remain, the method returns -1.
Complexity: The string is scanned once with expected O(1) dictionary and set operations, giving O(n) expected time and O(u) auxiliary space for u distinct characters.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest absolute path to a file in a newline-and-tab encoded directory listing.
Idea: Collect lines containing a dot as candidate files, then walk backward through the original listing to assemble their parent paths.
Technique and why it applies: Tab counts are used as directory depth; the code repeatedly searches earlier lines for the parent at each shallower depth, joins names with slashes, and returns the longest assembled path.
Invariant: Each entry in final is intended to contain one candidate file plus its ancestor directory names.
Edge cases: If input contains no dot, the method returns zero. Using '.' as a file test can misclassify directory names containing dots, and a.index(file) repeatedly finds the first equal line, which can be wrong for duplicate line text.
Complexity: Repeated list.index and backward scans can make time quadratic or worse in the number of lines; stored split lines, file lists, and paths use O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Compute the longest absolute file path length from a string where tabs encode directory depth and dots identify files.
Idea: Parse lines incrementally and keep the cumulative path length for each directory depth.
Technique and why it applies: path_len[d] stores the length of a directory path at depth d, including the separator needed for a child. A file at depth d is evaluated by adding its name length to path_len[d].
Invariant: Before processing each line, path_len contains the parent path length needed for the current depth, assuming the input hierarchy is valid.
Edge cases: If there are no file names containing a dot, max_len remains zero. A dot is the code's file indicator, as in the problem representation.
Complexity: Each input character is inspected a constant number of times, giving O(n) time. path_len stores lengths by depth, requiring O(d) auxiliary space, worst-case O(n); the author time label is consistent.

Task and constraints: Find the extra character in t, which is a shuffled copy of s with one additional character.
Idea: XOR the character codes from both strings together.
Technique and why it applies: XOR is associative and each value XORed with itself cancels to zero. Matching characters from s and t cancel regardless of order, leaving the code of the added character; chr converts it back to a one-character string.
Invariant: c equals the XOR of all codes processed so far, so after both loops it represents the unmatched character.
Edge cases: The problem guarantees exactly one added character, so the final XOR corresponds to one character code.
Complexity: Both strings are scanned once, giving O(m+n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the one character added to t after s has been shuffled and extended by one character.
Idea: Use reduce and XOR to combine the ordinal values of each string, then XOR those aggregates together.
Technique and why it applies: XOR cancellation removes every character present in both strings, independent of position. The remaining ordinal value is converted back to a character.
Invariant: Each reduce expression represents the XOR of all code points in its input string; their XOR is the unmatched code point.
Edge cases: The imports provide operator.xor, collections, and reduce; collections is unused. The input guarantee of exactly one extra character is necessary for interpretation.
Complexity: Mapping and reducing both strings takes O(m+n) time and O(1) auxiliary state beyond iterator objects; the expression does not build a character-count table.

Task and constraints: Find the final remaining number after repeatedly deleting alternating entries, reversing deletion direction each round.
Idea: Track the first surviving value, current spacing, remaining count, and deletion direction instead of constructing the list.
Technique and why it applies: The first surviving value advances by one current step when deleting from the left, or when deleting from the right with an odd count. Each round doubles spacing and halves the number of survivors.
Invariant: beg is the first surviving value, d is the distance between survivors, and len is the survivor count.
Edge cases: n=1 skips the loop and returns 1. The variable named len shadows Python's built-in len but is used only as a local integer.
Complexity: The survivor count halves each round, so time is O(log n) and auxiliary space is O(1).

Task and constraints: Return the last value left by alternating left-to-right and right-to-left elimination rounds.
Idea: Maintain the first surviving value, spacing between survivors, and direction of the next round.
Technique and why it applies: Each round halves n and doubles step. The start adjustment accounts for how many positions are removed and whether the first survivor moves forward or backward relative to the current direction.
Invariant: start is the first value in the current arithmetic progression of survivors; step is their spacing.
Edge cases: n=1 returns the initial start of 1. The loop runs until a single survivor remains.
Complexity: n is divided by two on every iteration, giving O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, consistent with the author labels.

Task and constraints: Decide whether the supplied axis-aligned rectangles form one exact rectangular cover with no gaps or overlaps.
Idea: Compare summed area with the bounding rectangle's area and use corner parity to verify only the four outer corners remain odd.
Technique and why it applies: Every rectangle contributes its area and toggles its four corners in a set. Shared internal corners cancel in pairs; the final set must contain exactly the bounding rectangle's four corners.
Invariant: points stores corners seen an odd number of times, while actual_area accumulates all rectangle areas.
Edge cases: Empty input is not handled because extrema remain infinities. The method assumes valid rectangles and checks both area equality and exact corner set membership.
Complexity: Each rectangle processes four corners, giving expected O(r) time and O(r) set space for r rectangles.

Task and constraints: Check whether axis-aligned rectangles exactly cover the bounding rectangular region.
Idea: Find the outer bounds and encode which corner directions occur at every coordinate point using bit masks.
Technique and why it applies: Each rectangle sets one of four bits at each corner; a repeated direction bit indicates an overlap and returns False. Interior points are then permitted only selected masks representing valid meeting patterns.
Invariant: points maps each encountered coordinate to the directional-corner mask accumulated there, with duplicate directional contributions rejected immediately.
Edge cases: The code assumes a nonempty rectangle list because min/max are called on generators. Its final interior-mask rule is the core correctness check, so unusual corner configurations depend on those allowed masks.
Complexity: Four corner updates per rectangle and a scan over unique corners give expected O(r) time and O(r) space for r rectangles.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s is a subsequence of t, preserving character order but allowing intervening characters.
Idea: Scan t and advance a pointer into s whenever the current characters match.
Technique and why it applies: subsequence counts how many leading characters of s have been matched in order. Once all characters match, the final equality returns True.
Invariant: The first subsequence characters have been matched to positions in t before the current scan position.
Edge cases: The early checks handle s longer than t and empty s. The code prints the next needed character during scanning, creating unwanted debug output but not changing the boolean result.
Complexity: The scan takes O(|t|) time and O(1) auxiliary space. The extra print calls can produce output proportional to the scan length.

Task and constraints: Return whether all characters of s can be matched in t from left to right.
Idea: Use one pointer into s while scanning each character of t once.
Technique and why it applies: On a match, advance i; characters that do not match are skipped. When i reaches len(s), every character has been found in order and the loop can stop early.
Invariant: s[:i] has been matched as a subsequence of the portion of t already scanned.
Edge cases: Empty s returns True immediately. The check for i == len(s) occurs before any later access to s[i], preventing an out-of-range access after the final match.
Complexity: Time is O(|t|) in the worst case and O(1) auxiliary space, matching the author labels when n denotes the length of t.

Task and constraints: Validate whether each integer in data forms a legal UTF-8 byte sequence under the stated leading- and continuation-bit rules.
Idea: Track how many continuation bytes are still expected after each multibyte leading byte.
Technique and why it applies: Leading-bit masks identify one-, two-, three-, or four-byte sequences. When continuation bytes are expected, each byte must begin with binary 10, after which the remaining count decreases.
Invariant: cont_bytes_left is the number of continuation bytes required before another leading byte may begin.
Edge cases: A sequence ending with a positive count is rejected. The code does not explicitly check that each input integer is in [0,255], so behavior for out-of-range values is outside its validation logic.
Complexity: Each byte is checked once, giving O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Determine whether the input integers encode a valid sequence of UTF-8 characters.
Idea: Use a counter for required continuation bytes and bit masks to classify leading bytes.
Technique and why it applies: With no pending continuation, leading bits select a sequence length or reject an invalid high bit. With a pending count, the byte must match the 10xxxxxx pattern, then the counter is decremented.
Invariant: count records how many continuation bytes must still arrive before the next character can start.
Edge cases: The final return rejects an incomplete multibyte character. The code assumes values represent bytes; it does not explicitly reject integers outside 0–255.
Complexity: Every element is processed once, so time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1), consistent with the author labels.
